+        # (pair -> idx dict, an id above every merge id) when the merge ids are
+        # distinct ints, so the lowest rank identifies a single pair; else None
+        lookup = self._get_merge_lookup()

+            self._merge_ranks_src = lookup
+        return self._merge_ranks

+    def _get_chunk_lookup(self):
+        ranks = self._get_merge_ranks()
+        return ranks if ranks is not None else self._get_merge_table()

+    def _encode_chunk(self, text_bytes, merge_lookup=None):
+        # return the token ids
+        # let's begin. first, convert all bytes to integers in range 0..255
+        ids = list(text_bytes)
+        if type(merge_lookup) is not list and type(merge_lookup) is not tuple:
+            merge_lookup = self._get_chunk_lookup()
+        if type(merge_lookup) is tuple:
+            # rank every adjacent pair in C and take the lowest one
+            ranks_get = merge_lookup[0].get
+            top = merge_lookup[1]
+            while len(ids) >= 2:
+                ranks = list(map(ranks_get, zip(ids, ids[1:]), repeat(top)))
+                best_idx = min(ranks)
+                if best_idx == top:
+                    break # nothing else can be merged anymore
+                i = ranks.index(best_idx)
+                if ranks.count(best_idx) == 1:
+                    # the pair occurs exactly once: merge it in place
+                    ids[i:i+2] = [best_idx]
+                    continue
+                best_p0 = ids[i]
+                best_p1 = ids[i+1]
+                newids = ids[:i]
+                append = newids.append
+                last = len(ids) - 1
+                while i < last:
+                    if ids[i] == best_p0 and ids[i+1] == best_p1:
+                        append(best_idx)
+                        i += 2
+                    else:
+                        append(ids[i])
+                        i += 1
+                if i == last:
+                    append(ids[i])
+                ids = newids
+            return ids
+        while len(ids) >= 2:

actions.reason: No encode_ir change reached the 1% bar; both measured variants made encode slower. (1) Ranking every adjacent pair in C per pass (map of merges.get over zip, then min/index/count) gave identical outputs but encode_ir 1.1514; with chunks this short, per-call overhead outweighs the Python scan. (2) A per-chunk rank list updating only the neighbouring pairs after each in-place merge gave identical outputs but encode_ir 1.0374. train_ir also rose in both runs (1.0074 and 1.0117) even though train never runs this code, which suggests that added source in regex.py costs instructions at import time. regex.py is back to the parent state. Not tried: cutting the per-chunk loop overhead for cache hits in encode_ordinary; estimated at well under 1%.

journal.text:
I worked on encode_ir in minbpe/regex.py, in the per-chunk merge loop. All edits were in that file.

The first variant ranked every adjacent pair in C on each pass with map of merges.get over zip, then min, index and count. Outputs were identical. encode_ir went from 409171687 to 471139347, ratio 1.1514. train_ir ratio was 1.0074. Rejected. The second variant kept a rank list per chunk and updated only the neighbouring pairs after each in-place merge. Outputs were identical. encode_ir was 424476527, ratio 1.0374, train_ir ratio 1.0117. Rejected. Neither change helped. I submitted no candidate.

I now think the chunks are too short for these approaches. The per-call overhead and the bookkeeping cost more than the plain Python scan they replace.

Next I want to look away from the inner merge loop. Two options are caching encoded chunks so repeated chunks skip merging, and cutting setup cost per chunk. I should measure how often chunks repeat before writing code.
